title: The eye does not go there
hookLine: the eye cannot go there, nor speech, nor the mind
carry: the image points; brahman is the one who sees

lines: THE ONE THING NEVER IN VIEW.
cards: Nobody has ever seen their own eyes. A mirror shows a picture of them. The actual eyes, the ones doing the seeing, stay out of sight: the one thing in the field of vision that can never be in the field of vision.
A tongue can't taste itself either. The Kena's next verses start from this puzzle. If Brahman is the eye of the eye, the eye will never see it.
And then the text says something that sounds almost shocking for a sacred book.

teach.h: THE EYE DOES NOT GO THERE.
teach.b: Verse three: the eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind. We don't know it; we don't understand how anyone could teach it.

teach.h: OTHER THAN THE KNOWN, BEYOND THE UNKNOWN.
teach.b: It is other than the known, and beyond the unknown. So we have heard from the ancients who explained it to us. The teacher can't hand this over like an object.
Then, in verses four to eight, a refrain comes five times. That which speech cannot express, but by which speech is expressed: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here.
That which the mind cannot think, but by which the mind thinks.
That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eyes see. The ear, the breath, the same. What does not this that people worship mean?

Commentators don't read it as throwing out worship. Hindus go right on worshiping. The point is sharper: whatever you can set in front of you as an object, even a holy one, is not the one doing the seeing.
Shankara reads it that way: Brahman is never an object among objects; it's the subject of all of them. So the murti on the home altar, the word in the prayer, can point to it.

teach.h: THE MURTI POINTS; IT CAN'T CONTAIN.

teach.b: That's how a Hindu can bow before a murti and still say God has no limit. Vedanta teachers have an old image for this. To show someone the faint star Arundhati, you first point to a bright star beside it.
The bright star helps, exactly as long as nobody stops there.

how: Hindus who study Vedanta often learn the Kena's refrain (1.4–1.8) as a teaching that Brahman is the knower, never an object known, alongside continuing worship of God in images and names.

o: the god who creates the world
the ultimate reality, ground of all

games.q: the Kena's refrain — tap the pairs.

s: the Kena tells Hindus to stop worshiping
commentators read it as: Brahman is never an object, not as a ban on worship.
the teacher admits he doesn't know how to teach it
verse three: we don't understand how anyone could teach it.
the refrain comes back five times
for speech, mind, eye, ear and breath.

games.q: a student asks the teacher to show him Brahman, just once, like an object. what does the Kena say?
o: 'the eye does not go there; it's what the eye sees by.'
games.why: the eye does not go there. Brahman is the one seeing, never one more thing seen.

practice: Look softly at something in front of you and notice all you can see; then, without moving your eyes, notice that the seeing happens from somewhere you can't see.
Close your eyes and do the same with a thought: watch it, and notice you can't turn around and watch the watcher. Rest in not being able to catch it.

wordCard.voice: Brahman, from brih, to grow, to be great. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eye sees: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here.

orig.note: Sanskrit: brahman, the ultimate reality; traditionally linked to brih, to grow, to be great.

carryVoice: Your line: the image points; brahman is the one who sees. The one looking is never in the picture. That's day two hundred forty-one.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 1.3 (the eye does not go there; other than the known)
Kena Upanishad 1.4–1.8 (know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship)
